items.title: 68088_Wilbur B. Ware, Sr oral history interview
items.q: Oh, well, Nicky Hill come up a little later.

ctx.x: Who were some of the other people that you played with at this time besides Ike Day and [Dorel] Anderson? Did you play with Wilbur Rubin Campbell at this time, Nicky Hill?

Oh, well, Nicky Hill come up a little later. Nicky Hill and Wilbur -- I guess Wilbur was playing around -- but I was working club dates -- and oh yeah, going back to this, I worked up at a place called the Argyle Show Lounge, up on the North Side. There was a tenor player named Gypsy -- a white tenor player. He loved Pres -- he played just like him. When I met Lee Konitz -- and oh, that piano player out of Chicago -- a whole lot of white Chicago musicians; I started getting gigs over there with these guys, you…

And they'd come on the South Side jam sessions, you know, and so I started getting jobs over there -- and oh, I had all kind of little gigs -- a gig here and a gig there. Different people. Chris Anderson Henderson, Van Vaughn Freeman ... the Freeman brothers; Van Buzz Buzz and George, and a piano player named Jo Jo Parnell.

items.title: 68088_Wilbur B. Ware, Sr oral history interview
items.q: I know bandleaders who tried to, you know, some cats they couldn't depend on, but they needed them because they could play. ... as well as Nicky Hill Gilbert could.

ctx.x: Well, even like Duke Ellington, with his -- he had a fantastic business sense along with his music, but even he had to have other people to help him. He just couldn't do everything else himself.

You can't, right. You go pick up the guys and ... I know bandleaders who tried to, you know, some cats they couldn't depend on, but they needed them because they could play. They would pick them up and do things like that just to make sure he would get to the gig on time. Even Leo. You know, Leo had a suit that I could wear it, as well as Nicky Hill Gilbert could. We didn't have a decent suit to look right on the bandstand, but Leo had his suit pressed, and I'd say there it is, and he made sure there were some…

But that was important, even up until the sixties. In the sixties, people started to, well, I can't really say not caring how they looked -- but they started looking like the general society looked. It wasn't important to dress up anymore in the sixties when you saw them up on the bandstand. In informal attire, but earlier on, you did have to look a certain way.
